key_points: A reprint of Jayaprakash Narayan's 1952 essay "Incentives for Goodness," republished as a tribute after his death on 17 September 1979, argues that modern materialism has eroded religion's traditional grounding for morality and that only transcending materialism, not any particular doctrine, can restore a durable incentive to goodness.

S. V. Raju's editorial column "Of Cabbages & Kings" reads the Sikkim election result as proof the 1975 merger referendum was manufactured, criticises the caretaker government for defending the 42nd Amendment in court despite N. A. Palkhivala's advocacy against it, and satirises the opportunistic pre-election alliances among Congress(U), Congress(I), Janata, Lok Dal, AIADMK, DMK, CPI and CPI(M).

A "Debate" section carries reader letters responding to Minoo Masani's "Haven't We Had Enough?", with contributors from Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra and Kerala split between backing independent candidates, blaming self-serving politicians rather than the constitution, and appealing to intellectuals for moral leadership.

Maj. Gen. E. D'Souza (Retd.) examines the Army-versus-Air Force dispute over control of Army Aviation helicopters, weighing the Army's case for tighter battlefield liaison against the Air Force's case for unified airspace control and cost, and concludes a separate Army Aviation arm is currently beyond India's economic means.

A reprinted Economist piece, "India Votes In (and for?) Freedom," frames the coming general election as offering no clear policy choice despite India's remarkable record of resolving crises, including the 1975-77 Emergency, through the ballot, and asks whether it will restore power to the hands whose earlier abuse of it voters had condemned.

Russian dissident Vladimir Bukovsky's "The Moscow Olympics" argues the Soviet Union fails the IOC's own standards of political stability and non-discrimination, citing occupation of the Baltic states, KGB vetting of athletes, and restricted access to Soviet Jews, and calls holding the Games in Moscow a betrayal.

Muriel Wasi reviews Stephan Alter's novel Neglected Lives, praising its sympathetic, multi-narrator portrait of Lucknow's Anglo-Indian community and its refusal to caricature Anglo-Indian identity and sexuality.

Padmini Murti reviews S. Radhakrishnan's Indian Religions, highlighting his argument that no religion can claim superiority over others and that cross-fertilisation among traditions, once outdated ritual is stripped away, enriches spiritual life.

The Special Number, marking S. V. Raju and Geeta Doctor's handover of the editorship to Nissim Ezekiel, is devoted entirely to "The Crisis and Challenge of Leadership in Modern Society," with an unsigned editorial framing India's problems as fundamentally a crisis of character in its leadership.

S. P. Aiyar's "The Riddle of Leadership" argues no single typology survives historical variety and treats charismatic leadership as dangerous, citing Indira Gandhi's Emergency-era isolation among sycophants as a cautionary example.

M. R. Masani's "Two Styles of Leadership" blames India's leadership shortage on a cultural deference to age and a "dialectical" reluctance to commit to clear positions, contrasting Churchill and De Gaulle's conditional leadership with Morarji Desai and Charan Singh's premierships.

R. M. Lala's "Leadership Yesterday and Today" argues the burdens of jet travel, mass communication and unrelenting scrutiny have made modern leadership far harder than in Gladstone's day, citing the Shah of Iran's isolation from expert advice as a cautionary case.

S. K. Ookerjee's "Recipe for Making Leaders" dismisses formal leadership training as impossible since leadership is a matter of character rather than technical skill, warning against both dictatorial figures like Hitler and Idi Amin and the surrender of followers' own moral judgement.

Taya Zinkin's "The Civil Servant as a Leader" argues efficiency must precede honesty and impartiality in public administration, illustrating "leading by example" with the story of Collector Captain Mohite of Sholapur, whose development gains collapsed once he was transferred.

M. R. Masani's "Another Chance for Mrs. Gandhi" analyses Congress (I)'s 1980 landslide, arguing its 66.85% parliamentary majority on only 42.58% of the vote reflects the distorting first-past-the-post system rather than a personal mandate, and calls for proportional representation and a policy agenda of tax cuts, decontrol and restraint from vindictiveness.

A. E. Gunawardena's "The Experience of Absolutism in Ceylon" reviews Sri Lanka's 1977 election as a warning of how an unchecked two-thirds parliamentary majority let Sirimavo Bandaranaike's government abolish the Senate and undermine judicial independence and press freedom.

Three "Voices" pieces address Communist bloc economic weakness, citing steep 1979 fuel-price rises across Poland, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria, a proposal that Indian parties run internal intelligence units to curb corruption and defections, and a post-mortem on the non-Congress opposition's "bulldozer" defeat blaming Indira Gandhi's charisma, administrative discontent and Charan Singh's inflationary budget.

C. L. Proudfoot's "Changing Values in Sports" laments the decline of amateur "Skill and Joy" sporting values in India against cricket's television-driven commercialisation and the closure of the Anglo-Indian schools that once nurtured hockey talent.

The World of Books section reviews Krishnabai Nimbkar's Emergency-era prison diary, M. N. Rudrabasavaraj's Dynamic Personnel Administration, and Bruce M. Swain's Reporters' Ethics on the gap between journalistic myth and reality.

Editor Nissim Ezekiel's closing essay condemns the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan as unambiguous aggression, rejecting arguments that criticism would "escalate" tension and weighing responses including an Olympics boycott and revision of India's Soviet friendship treaty.

S. V. Raju's "Assemblies Dissolved" accuses Mrs. Gandhi's Congress (I) government of repeating, in 1980, the same dissolution of nine opposition-ruled state assemblies that Janata had used against its opponents in 1977, exploiting a Supreme Court precedent Janata itself had set.

The Hindustani Andolan's "Blue-Print for National Reconciliation" sets out preconditions for cross-party reconciliation, including depoliticised justice, decontrol of production, a non-partisan family-planning effort, and a crackdown on election-expense-driven corruption.

Three "Voices" pieces cover Nissim Ezekiel's confession that decades of intellectual ferment have not translated into real institutional change, Preethi Biddapa's survey of the global revival of Islam as a reaction to Western-linked modernisation, and Shama Futehally's critique of a Bombay textbook that favours moralising content over literary merit.

V. B. Karnik's "Our Trade Unions" urges Indian unions to abandon confrontational militancy for negotiation, coalition-building and outreach to unorganised and rural labour, citing the British Social Contract and US AFL-CIO accord as models.

Geeta Doctor's satirical "Encounters of the Southern Kind" recounts Madras elites boasting of never voting, women reportedly given sarees to skip voting for outgoing chief minister MGR, and a servant boy wrongfully detained by police and released only after a bribe-like payment.

The World of Books section reviews five titles including Sean Kelly's Access Denied on press censorship, Jamila Verghese's Her Gold and Her Body on dowry, and Mario Miranda and Rajan Narayan's cartoon book Elections Indian Style, alongside a sharp critique of Jagjit Singh Anand's pro-Soviet Indo-Soviet Relations.
The issue closes with the Liberal International's Messina statement condemning the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan and the internal exile of Andrei Sakharov as violations of the Helsinki Agreements.

Nissim Ezekiel's editorial "Mrs. Gandhi & Sanjay" warns that Indira Gandhi has shown no change in method since returning to power and that a Sanjay Gandhi succession would pose an even graver, harder-to-resist authoritarian threat.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "Press Freedom and Official Secrets" contrasts India's unreformed Official Secrets Act, 1923 with Britain's Franks Committee reforms and the US Freedom of Information Act, calling for review in light of India's obligations under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.

Anita Sethi's "That Hell Called Cuba," with a reprinted OAS human-rights report, documents torture and over 470 deaths among roughly 1,000 Cuban political "plantados" and contrasts Cuba's economic collapse with Chile's growth under Pinochet's economist Sergio de Castro.

Eduard Neumaier's "Kremlin Shuts the Gate" argues the Soviet Union has offered no genuine concessions in the three months since invading Afghanistan, dismissing Lord Carrington's neutralisation plan and reading Soviet "contradictions" as a deliberate stalling tactic.

Two "Voices" pieces cover Rama Swarup's argument that three decades of Chinese Communist rule produced destructive upheaval rather than real development, and Nitin G. Raut's criticism of India's diplomatic recognition of the PLO office in Delhi as inconsistent given its refusal of full relations with Israel.

The World of Books section reviews six titles, including R. M. Lala on Manohar Malgonkar's Cue From The Inner Voice on business trusteeship from Tata to Gandhi to JP, and critical notices of Balwant Gargi's memoir, a prison memoir, P. Lal's poem "Calcutta," and a small-industries study.

Aloo Dalal opens a two-part investigative series on India's municipal governments, tracing their origins to the Bombay Acts of 1865-1888 and cataloguing the financial and legal weaknesses that leave them unable to keep pace with rapid urbanisation.

Nissim Ezekiel's editorial "After the Elections" argues that fear, not disagreement, now shapes public reaction to criticism of Mrs. Gandhi and Sanjay Gandhi, warning of an unaccountable "Power behind the powers" while insisting a working democracy remains preferable to any authoritarian alternative.

Singapore Foreign Minister S. Rajaratnam's reprinted Tokyo speech, "Soviet World in the Making," argues detente has systematically favoured Soviet expansion into Vietnam, Cuba, Angola, Ethiopia, Mozambique, South Yemen, Kampuchea and Afghanistan through Western self-deception rather than Soviet trickery.

Two "Voices" pieces address a Maharashtra circular letting colleges self-declare "minority" status to bypass merit admissions, and Rahul Singh's warning, drawn from South Korea's 1980 political violence, against Indian intellectuals romanticising authoritarian "strong leadership."

A joint statement from the Bombay Rationalist Association reproduces the 192-scientist "Objections to Astrology" declaration and calls on newspapers to stop publishing horoscopes as corrosive to rational, self-reliant citizenship.

A short news item reports a World Bank finding that modern hospital-based health systems bypass 80 per cent of the poor in developing countries, prompting the Bank's first direct financing of health projects.

The World of Books section reviews Ved Mehta's biography Daddyji and the fourth edition of Jadunath Sarkar's House of Shivaji, which the reviewer credits with correcting earlier dismissive views of Shivaji.

Attar Chand's "Let Us Remember Rural Poverty" cites World Bank data placing India among a "fourth world" of impoverishing countries and warns of a potential "explosive class-war" unless rural priorities shift, while Aloo Dalal concludes her two-part series on municipalities by warning that Bombay's Corporation could be the next target of central government supersession after Delhi's.

Nissim Ezekiel's editorial on "Sanjay's Death - & After" argues Sanjay Gandhi's political rise rested on scandal and cult rather than achievement, calling his politics "crypto-fascist," and criticises Indira Gandhi's government for echoing Soviet propaganda on the Afghanistan invasion.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "Amnesty's Indictment of Soviet Savagery" details Amnesty International's report on Soviet political prisoners, citing the cases of Balys Gajankas and poetess Yuliya Okulova and the abuse of psychiatric confinement to silence dissenters.

The Iranian Committee for Democratic Action and Human Rights' open letter to Austria's Chancellor Bruno Kreisky protests his Tehran visit, citing over 1,200 executions without fair trial and 50,000 political prisoners under Khomeini's theocracy.

Two "Voices" pieces cover A. E. Gunawardena's argument that capitalist inflation is a "myth" in efficient Western democracies, and Hutoxi Mehenti's first-person account of the gap between a promised "challenging" office job and the reality of routine clerical work.

Geeta Doctor's satirical "The Week In Parliament" imagines MPs demanding caste quotas on Nobel-laureate sperm donations, with the twist that the disguised fifth candidate turns out to be the Prime Minister herself.

The World of Books section reviews Barun Sengupta's exposé of the Janata government's collapse, Surabhi Sheth's study of the Brahma Purana, Gail Omvedt's account of Maharashtra women workers, and Lord Denning's The Due Process of Law.

Jonathan Fenby's "Third World Aversion To Bad News" largely debunks the thesis that Western media disproportionately emphasise Third World disasters, citing a University of North Carolina study finding disaster coverage a small share of total news everywhere.

S. K. Ookerjee opens an "Investigations" series on higher education, examining Bombay University's new lecture-attendance rules and proposing a three-semester structure and greater pedagogic freedom for teachers.

Nissim Ezekiel's editorial "The Moral Imperative" calls on individual Indians to embody liberal values in daily conduct through self-criticism and small constructive acts rather than relying on absent political leadership.

K. V. Subrahmanyam's "The Politics of Non-Renewable Resources" traces Soviet resource-driven interventions from Eastern Europe through Cuba, Guinea, Chile and Angola to bauxite deposits in Orissa-Andhra Pradesh, linking the invasion of Afghanistan to the region's untapped gas fields.

William Frankel profiles Statesman managing director Cushrow Irani, the first Indian chairman of the International Press Institute, recounting his defiance of Emergency-era government pressure including passport impoundment and threats to nationalise newspaper ownership.

Andrei Sakharov's message to the International Sakharov Hearings argues Soviet law itself, not merely its abuse, violates human rights, citing the death penalty for non-violent offences and the "anti-parasite law."

A three-part "Voices" column covers the neglect of deaf education in India, satire of performative bohemianism in Baroda's arts scene, and the WHO's October 1980 declaration that smallpox has been eradicated worldwide.

The World of Books section reviews Indira Mahindra's The Rebellious Home-Makers on Indian women's domestic resistance and the Sunday Times Insight Team's account of the 1980 Iranian Embassy siege in London.
An essay on "End of the Olympics" argues the Moscow Games boycott exposes the fiction that sport and politics can be separated, tracing politicised Olympics back to Berlin 1936.

Thomas Hamm's reprinted profile of Truong Nhu Tang, a founding NLF member turned boat-person exile, describes Vietnam's Communist Party betraying its nationalist ideals and its near-total dependence on Soviet aid.

S. K. Ookerjee's continuing "Investigations" essay argues the college teacher should be an explorer of ideas rather than a mere instructor, criticising large lecture classes and calling tutorials "the harijans of our system."

Nissim Ezekiel's editorial "The Communal Virus" argues communal violence is rooted in fanaticism and insecurity within each religious community rather than simple inter-group friction, and criticises reservation-driven identity politics for deepening rather than resolving it.

P. M. Kamath's "India's Sterile Afghan Policy" criticises India's abstention on the UN resolution condemning the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and calls for India to press for unconditional Soviet withdrawal and a UN peacekeeping force on Afghanistan's borders.

K. M. Pathak's "American Public Moods and Mr. Carter's Re-Election" surveys the volatility of US opinion toward President Carter ahead of the 1980 election, citing his Panama Canal and Camp David achievements against the damage done by inflation and the Iran hostage crisis.

Two "Voices" pieces reproduce Alexander Solzhenitsyn's Foreign Affairs warning against conflating Communist regimes with their peoples and an argument that US courtship of Communist China abandons Taiwan and the mainland Chinese people.
A satirical short story follows a housewife who, after years internalising contradictory ideals from women's magazines, burns her collection in an act read as liberation.
Book reviews cover Brian Crozier's Strategy of Survival on Soviet expansionism and Shridath Ramphal's One World to Share on North-South economic dialogue.

Features profile the Vigil India Movement's grassroots defence of democracy and secularism, the Academy of Development Science at Kikwi bridging university and rural learners, and the Committee for the Protection of Democratic Rights' "Know Your Rights" handbook founded in reaction to the Emergency.

Vasant K. Bawa reports on the "Agenda for India" conference proposing decentralisation, electoral reform and freeing media from state control, while Attar Chand's "Our Scientists Abroad" estimates 200,000 Indian technical professionals working overseas and calls for stronger research investment to curb the brain drain.

Nissim Ezekiel's editorial "Backdoor Emergency" condemns the National Security Ordinance's due-process failures and the Maruti nationalisation, following the A. C. Gupta Commission's findings of irregularities, as evidence of a "backdoor Emergency" under Indira Gandhi.

Dutch MP F. Bolkestein's Berlin speech, "Soviet Imperialism and Western Strategy," sets out five Western objectives on Afghanistan and argues detente must be paired with Western rearmament, citing Helmut Schmidt and the Sakharov case before the Hague tribunal.

J. G. Tiwari's "Soviet Imperialism and Poland's Revolt" credits the Gdansk agreement's concessions to Polish workers, and the emergence of KOR, the Church and independent intellectuals, as a historic step toward pluralism the Soviet leadership has so far tolerated.

Y. Shivaji's "Soviet Imperialism and India's Stance" argues India's recognition of the Heng Samrin regime and muted response to Afghanistan reveal a foreign policy that flatters Moscow and has hollowed non-alignment into mere economic backwardness.

A three-part "Voices" column covers rural sewage and pollution neglect, the pervasiveness of everyday bribery from school admissions to Lockheed-style scandals, and criticism of the Maharashtra Chief Minister's suggestion that judges should not interpret the Constitution.

The World of Books section reviews Bipan Chandra's Marxian Nationalism and Colonialism in Modern India, Meira Chand's novel The Gossamer Fly, and poetry collections by Sunita Jain and Meena Alexander.

K. V. Subrahmanyam's "Right and Wrong in Politics" traces the search for an objective political morality from Orwell and ancient religious ethics through Bertrand Russell, arguing pluralist self-governing institutions, not written constitutions alone, sustain democratic order, and closing with a critique of Gandhi's "imaginary ideals" and Nehru's admiration for Stalin's nationalities policy.

Nissim Ezekiel's editorial "Democratic Republic" argues that one-party states appropriating the language of democracy suppress dissent and control press and judiciary to preserve their monopoly on "truth," and that citing social achievements like housing and health does not answer the denial of basic civil liberties.

K. S. Venkateswaran's two-part "Justice Krishna Iyer" accuses the recently retired Supreme Court judge of substituting florid rhetoric for judicial restraint, quoting H. M. Seervai's charge that Iyer's concept of the judicial function was "subversive" of the Constitution.

Milovan Djilas's "Eurocommunist Delusions" criticises Enrico Berlinguer and Santiago Carrillo for equating the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan with alleged US misdeeds, and extends the critique to Yugoslav officials who, fearing Soviet reprisal, adopt a similarly evasive "non-aligned" framing.

Cushrow Irani's UNESCO address, "Free Press Or Enslaved Press?", argues against the MacBride Commission's proposed "new information order" for wrongly linking press freedom to economic development and risking government control of journalism.

Short reports announce the founding of the JP Forum for Total Revolution at Rajghat, Varanasi, and a Radical Humanist Association resolution criticising both Janata and Congress governments for failing to solve poverty and warning against a drift toward presidential dictatorship.

Three "Voices" pieces cover a satire on shifting Indian attitudes to foreign visitors, a warning about opaque, poorly-regulated foreign fund flows into Indian associations, and a critique of a Films Division documentary that trivialises India's sanitation crisis.

Book reviews cover P. S. Jha's political economy of Indian stagnation, Henry Scott Stokes's biography of Yukio Mishima, Asghar Ali Engineer's history of Islam, and a Nehru Memorial Museum symposium volume comparing Gandhi and Nehru's economic thought.

Two companion essays on "The Educational Mess" describe the bureaucratic ordeal facing Maharashtra parents reconciling the I.C.S.E. and state education boards, and criticise Indian universities as impersonal "graduate-producing factories" lacking a unifying purpose.

Nissim Ezekiel's editorial "The Brezhnev Visit" condemns the Indo-Soviet communique following Brezhnev's December 1980 visit for omitting any mention of Afghanistan, arguing Mrs. Gandhi traded India's non-aligned credibility for Soviet oil and arms.

Pran Nath Lekhi's "The Brezhnev Doctrine: A Grand Design?" traces Soviet doctrine from the 1968 justification of the Czechoslovakia invasion through the 1978 Soviet-Afghan Treaty to Brezhnev's Persian Gulf "peace" proposal, questioning its selective application.

A report describes the founding of the People's Union of Civil Liberties at a contentious Delhi conference chaired by V. M. Tarkunde, which passed resolutions against the National Security Ordinance and preventive detention.
Two "Voices" pieces cover the neglect of India's cerebrally palsied population and an eight-point programme for rural development and decentralisation.
The World of Books reviews M. Hidayatullah's reticent memoir My Own Boswell, an uneven poetry anthology, a study of K. M. Munshi, and P. G. Mavalankar's Emergency-era Parliament speeches.

An analytical piece catalogues the USSR's network of friendship treaties with Third World states from Egypt and India (1971) to South Yemen (1979), reading their "consultation" clauses as echoing Warsaw Pact obligations.

P. M. Kamath's "De Facto Presidential Government in India" argues President Sanjiva Reddy's handling of the July 1979-January 1980 political crisis, including Charan Singh's unconfirmed caretaker premiership, amounted to an unaccountable de facto presidential system.

Nissim Ezekiel's "The Two Super-Powers" argues that despite America's flaws its open, self-correcting society cannot be morally equated with Soviet totalitarian closure, even amid a more confrontational Reagan-era posture.

R. V. Sen's "Cruelty in Indian Society" argues that the Bhagalpur police blindings and Samastipur killings are dramatic instances of an everyday authoritarian cruelty pervading Indian police stations, schools, homes and workplaces.

Arvind Deshpande's "People's Action" reports on a Bombay planning meeting that resolved to organise a national convention on civil liberties, decentralisation and resisting authoritarianism in the post-JP era.

Bayard Rustin's reprinted "Workers and Democracy" frames the 1980 Polish strikes as a struggle to democratise an authoritarian society through independent trade unions, warning that Soviet pressure could still reverse the settlement.

A three-part "Voices" column covers a complaint about India's degree-fetishising education system, a critique of a condescending children's religious magazine, and a report on a talk tracing the history of women's education from Raja Ram Mohan Roy onward.
Book reviews cover a booklet on the Dawoodi Bohra priesthood's near-feudal authority, an anthology of Indian-English prose, and Bapsy Sidhwa's novel The Crow Eaters.

The issue reprints Paul Kurtz's 1980 "Secular Humanist Declaration" in full, laying out ten principles including free inquiry, church-state separation and religious scepticism against fundamentalist and authoritarian ideologies.

Nissim Ezekiel's editorial questions the moral coherence of non-alignment, criticising India's muted response to the Vietnamese occupation of Kampuchea and the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan despite its claimed moral leadership.

K. S. Venkateswaran summarises Amnesty International's 1979-80 annual report, including its aide-memoire to Mrs Gandhi's government criticising misuse of preventive detention and prison conditions at Tihar Jail.

J. G. Tiwari analyses a Soviet pamphlet, The Truth About Afghanistan, showing it frames Pakistan's military as complicit in suppressing "liberation struggle" and condemns Iran and Khomeini for anti-Soviet rhetoric.

C. Raju's "Dilemmas Of Liberty" argues that concentration of economic power, in the state or in monopolistic private hands, is liberty's central threat, citing Milton Friedman's Capitalism and Freedom.
Homai Moos describes the London-founded Child-to-Child Programme's Indian chapters, which train older children to assist younger ones' health and welfare, with its 1981 focus on handicapped children.

The World of Books reviews the H. M. Patel commemoration volume, Ved Mehta's family memoir Mamaji, an anthology of contemporary Indian English verse, and a study of women's labour exploitation across Japan, Malaysia and India.

M. A. Rane's tribute to the late M. C. Chagla recalls his defiance of MISA-era restrictions during the Emergency, his presidency of Citizens for Democracy after JP's death, and his lifelong rationalism, including a cremation without religious rites.

Nissim Ezekiel's editorial "How To Destroy The Unity of India" warns that separatism, citing Kashmir specifically, and the political appeasement of minority groups for votes threaten India's national integrity.

Arvind Deshpande's "The Reservation Trap" argues caste-based reservation alone cannot address backward-class deprivation without social acceptance, calling instead for job creation and invoking Ambedkar's emphasis on self-respect over legislative remedy.

An unsigned piece, "The dead cannot protest," accuses politicians who opposed Rajaji and JP in life of opportunistically claiming affinity with them in death, singling out the invitation of socialist James Callaghan to a Rajaji memorial lecture as a stark irony.

Smita Bankeshwar's "Gandhian Socialism" argues the phrase is a contradiction in terms, criticising Rajaji's trusteeship doctrine as intellectually evasive since it rests on an untested wish that the rich will behave altruistically.

A three-part "Voices" column covers intellectuals' responsibility in the nuclear age, a review of a Gujarati anthology on singer-composer Pankaj Mullick, and a review of a Cambridge Theatre Company production of Macbeth in Bombay.

Mehra Masani's polemic against the government's control of All India Radio and Doordarshan argues genuine broadcasting professionalism is impossible so long as civil-service staffing and bureaucratic budget control override independent editorial judgement.
Book reviews cover a critical study of Nirad C. Chaudhuri and Dilip Chitre's debut English poetry collection Travelling in a Cage.

Pratima Asher interviews sociologist Dr. Neera Desai of S.N.D.T.'s Women's Studies Research Unit, who distinguishes women's studies from an "anti-man" feminism and describes an action programme in nine South Gujarat villages.

M. R. Masani's "Life or Death: The Freedom to Choose" argues the right to die is a fundamental right alongside the right to live, prompted by the assisted death of 85-year-old Poona resident Gopal Mandlik, and invites readers to help found an Indian right-to-die society.

Anita Sethi's "Brezhnev's New Suggestion" analyses Brezhnev's Persian Gulf proposal as a strategic move to ease Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan while ultimately aiming to force Western withdrawal from the Gulf.

P. M. Kamath's "Parliamentary Democracy or Presidential Dictatorship?" examines the case made by A. R. Antulay, Nani Palkhivala and J. R. D. Tata for switching to presidential government, concluding it risks individual dictatorship given India's weak checks and balances.

Two "Voices" pieces cover a critical report on a Tribal Arts seminar in the Dangs that sidelined actual Dangi performers, and supply-side prescriptions for controlling inflation through boosting domestic production.
Book reviews cover Asghar Ali Engineer's The Bohras and a satirically panned translated Tamil novel, Metamorphosis.
Reader Radha Shrivastava reproduces Malcolm Muggeridge's polemic against Soviet apologists, prompted by the revival of "Friends of the Soviet Union" groups among Indian MPs.

The International League for Human Rights details the UN Human Rights Commission's repeated deferral of the Andrei Sakharov case, while a Vigil India Movement report describes eighty-three Women's Vigil Groups organising in Kanya Kumari district, and a PUCL Bombay resolution condemns the National Security Act.
Nissim Ezekiel attacks Rajiv Gandhi's entry into politics as a stage-managed extension of Indira Gandhi's dynastic control, resting on maternal patronage rather than independent achievement.

B. P. Adarkar's "The Chinese Conundrum" argues Nehru's non-alignment was internally contradictory, blaming Khrushchev for misleading Nehru into the 1962 border war over the strategically worthless Aksai Chin.

A reprint of the Indian Liberal Group's 1975 statement condemns the Emergency's censorship and MISA detentions as exceeding colonial-era repression, calling for free elections and restored press freedom.

Arvind A. Deshpande defends Gandhian trusteeship over common ownership, invoking Maslow and Schumacher on self-actualisation and describing a common-ownership model from England and Spain with capped wage differentials.

A report on Soviet policy toward Islam describes suppressed mosques and restricted seminaries in Bokhara and Tashkent despite a 1981 Soviet Muslim delegation sent to South Yemen to counter accusations of anti-Islamic policy.

Two "Voices" pieces cover a review of Arun Gandhi's book on apartheid South Africa, A Patch of White, and a report on Citizens for Democracy resolutions endorsing JP-committee electoral reforms including state funding of elections.

Book reviews cover a seminar booklet on Indian press freedom constraints and Keki Daruwalla's poetry collection Winter Poems, while a companion essay surveys global population growth and its strain on food and employment in developing nations.

Nissim Ezekiel's "Communist Doctrines — Illusion and Reality" catalogues asymmetries between communist and Western civil liberties, arguing the USSR claims an unchallengeable right of intervention in its "sphere of influence" while denying reciprocal rights to others.

Rahul Singh's "The Rule of the Gun" surveys a spate of 1981 political assassinations and terrorism worldwide, judging India comparatively free of such violence and crediting Indian democracy's absorption of former extremists like West Bengal's Marxists and the DMK.
S. S. Bankeshwar's "Chavan: The Lost Leader" attacks Y. B. Chavan's rejoining of Congress(I) as opportunism dressed as "Home Coming," coining the term "Chavanism" for political fence-sitting.
M. R. Masani's tribute to the late S. K. Patil recalls his devotion to Bombay's civic life and his "Live and Let Live" tolerance as a rare liberal trait in Indian politics.

A comment piece alleges a new protocol between the Congress(I)-backed Friends of the Soviet Union and its Soviet counterpart enables covert influence, criticising CSIR Vice-President Nurul Hasan's signing of it and alleged Marxist recruitment at Jawaharlal Nehru University.

A review of R. M. Lala's The Creation of Wealth, a Tata-commissioned defence of free enterprise, cites figures on Tata's real asset growth and JRD Tata's 1979 memorandum asserting Board, not family, control.

Shorter items cover a multi-signatory statement on India's population explosion, a Bhagalpur police-blinding cover-up allegedly funded by local businessmen, the launch of the Sarvodaya Press Service for rural news, the inauguration of Ahmedabad's Consumer Education and Research Centre, and a profile of Bombay's Maratha Mandir welfare institution.

Nissim Ezekiel's "Martyrs of Maharashtra" attacks the state government's plan for 204 costly Martyrs' Memorials while pavement-dwellers are evicted during the monsoon, calling the Chief Minister's style "management by muddle."

K. V. Subramanyam's "The Ways of Soviet Neo-colonialism" traces Soviet "switch trade" extraction of Indian mica, groundnut oil-cake, tobacco and foodgrains via non-convertible rupee balances back to Hjalmar Schacht's Nazi-era trade methods.

An unsigned report on Amnesty International's engagement with Vietnam's "re-education" camps describes 20,000 prisoners still held as of September 1980 and details individual cases of indefinite detention without trial.

Zena Sorabjee's "Persecution of the Baha'is in Iran" documents intensifying state-backed persecution of Iran's roughly 500,000-strong Baha'i community, including the destruction of its holiest shrine in Shiraz and executions for "teaching the Baha'i Faith."

Rashmi Taneja's "Russia's Dilemma" analyses the Solidarity-driven crisis in Poland, framing Brezhnev's choice between military intervention and tolerating reform as a catch-22 given uncertain army loyalty.
PUCL resolutions condemn rising preventive detention, attacks on judicial independence, press intimidation and Karnataka's interception of citizens' postal mail.

Sampath S. Iyengar's "Unemphasized Issues in Economics" argues decades of Indian planning failed to reduce poverty because markets structurally favour those with prior capital and power, invoking Schumacher's critique of economics based on "envy and greed."

P. M. Kamath's "Indo-Pak Relations" surveys India-Pakistan relations through superpower rivalry, concluding India needs Pakistan as a buffer state and should offer a no-war pact contingent on Pakistan accepting India's position on Kashmir.

Nissim Ezekiel's "The Judiciary and Mrs. Gandhi" indicts the government for deliberately transferring and superseding judges whose verdicts went against it, framing an independent judiciary as essential to a non-tyrannical polity.

Rashmi Taneja's "The Neutron Bomb" examines the NATO backlash to Reagan's decision to produce the radiation-heavy weapon, warning it could alienate European publics and hand the Soviet Union a propaganda advantage.

K. V. Subrahmanyam's "India's One Party Democracy" traces Congress's post-Independence dominance to Nehru's admiration for the Soviet model and adult franchise without literacy requirements, crediting Ambedkar alone among the framers with foreseeing the risks.

Two "Voices" pieces cover a polemic against Janata Party mergers and defections, and a report on India's high maternal and infant mortality and worsening sex ratio, contrasting Kerala's better outcomes with high female literacy.
Book reviews cover Bimal Prasad's edited volume of JP's writings tracing his evolution from Marxism to Sarvodaya and Total Revolution, and Taya Zinkin's guide to English communication, Write Right.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "A Variety of Comment" covers Indian media's hypocritical reaction to Britain's 1981 race riots, praise for the US "right to work" movement against forced unionism, and scepticism toward India's "Health for All" nationalisation proposal.

Short notices announce the Centre for the Independence of Judges and Lawyers, formed in Geneva, and report on Common Cause's advocacy for urban middle-class grievances including a Supreme Court writ petition on pensioner discrimination.

Nissim Ezekiel's editorial accuses the non-aligned movement of a double standard, readily condemning Israel, South Africa and the US while staying silent on Soviet aggression in Afghanistan and Poland.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "A Variety of Comment" reads the Antulay scandal as proof of concentrated state power's corrupting potential, argues squatters lack a "fundamental right" to occupy Bombay's pavements, and marshals statistics to defend infant-formula manufacturers against the anti-formula campaign.

Y. Sivaji's "Threats to Liberal Democracy" surveys how post-colonial "socialist" strongmen like Sukarno and Nkrumah eroded democracy through Soviet-style planning, calling for decentralisation and a mixed economy instead.
Two "Voices" pieces review Sam Shepard's Pulitzer-winning play Buried Child staged in Bombay and question whether India's and Britain's exam-driven education systems truly reward merit.
Book reviews cover A. B. Shah's Religion and Society in India, which rejects Radhakrishnan's model of secularism as equal state patronage of all religions, and B. R. Nanda's biography Mahatma Gandhi.

Buchung K. Tsering's "The Tragedy of the Tibetan People" surveys twenty-two years of Chinese rule over Tibet, criticising the UN's ineffectiveness and affirming non-violence as the appropriate Tibetan strategy despite admiring the PLO's ability to draw attention to its cause.

Nissim Ezekiel's "Bulgaria and Reality" accuses Indira Gandhi of ideological evasiveness on her Bulgaria visit, arguing her calls for "sovereign equality" ignore Bulgaria's total subservience to Soviet power.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "A Variety of Comment" criticises praise for Soviet legal "efficiency," endorses Subramaniam Swamy's charge that India's West Asia policy is self-defeating hypocrisy, and reports the unexplained absence of a Soviet physicist from an international conference as evidence of restricted academic freedom.

Rashmi Taneja's "Why Sadat Was Killed" traces the political causes of Anwar Sadat's assassination to his economic liberalisation, the Camp David accords' isolation of Egypt from the Arab world, and a crackdown that swept up 1,500 people a month before his death.
A companion piece by Arvind A. Deshpande criticises Indira Gandhi's description of Sadat as an "unpopular" Western-propped leader as ungracious toward a courageous ally.

A review of Aparna Sen's directorial debut 36 Chowringhee Lane reads Jennifer Kendal's portrayal of an ageing Anglo-Indian schoolteacher as a meditation on loneliness and the community's post-independence decline.

Praja R. Parekh argues, citing the Ramayana, Mahabharata and figures like Adi Shankaracharya, that India's law criminalising suicide reflects Macaulay's Christian assumptions rather than Hindu tradition, which he says has never condemned voluntary death.
A. Solomon's tribute to the late humanist scholar A. B. Shah praises his fearless critical study of Islam, motivated by a desire for Muslims' social emancipation rather than hostility.

P. M. Kamath's essay on Indian federalism argues over-centralisation, not federal structure itself, is the core problem, tracing it to Mrs. Gandhi's dual role as Prime Minister and Congress(I) party president.
Nissim Ezekiel's "Lies About Poland" argues Western and Indian commentary on Poland has been captured by propaganda recasting Soviet-backed repression of Solidarity as a legitimate internal matter.

P. N. Lekhi's "Betrayal of Poland" traces Polish worker uprisings from Poznan 1956 to Solidarity's 1980 founding, drawing an explicit parallel between General Jaruzelski's martial-law broadcast and Indira Gandhi's 1975 Emergency broadcast.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "A Variety of Comment" covers the erosion of judicial integrity after two Delhi High Court judges were not confirmed, questions a Maharashtra circular mandating a patriotic pledge in colleges, and notes P. G. Wodehouse's neglected Indian centenary.

Three "Voices" pieces cover Jonas Savimbi's UNITA movement in Angola, a critical review of a Doordarshan poetry programme, and a satire on communal double standards toward Muslims voicing political criticism.
Rashmi Taneja's "Major Change in British Politics" analyses Shirley Williams's Crosby by-election win for the new SDP-Liberal Alliance as a sign Britain's two-party system may be ending.
Book reviews cover Humayun Kabir's reissued novel Men and Rivers and Vaikom Basheer's story collection Me Grandad 'Ad an Elephant.
A Sarvodaya Press Service report describes Raj Inqalab, a Bihar-movement activist held without trial and on a years-long fast in Bhagalpur jail, warning his death could trigger unrest.

Nissim Ezekiel's "A Chief Minister as Clown" argues Maharashtra's Babasaheb Bhosale and his predecessor A. R. Antulay reveal usually concealed Indian political attitudes, citing Bhosale's public deification of Indira Gandhi as a goddess.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "A Variety of Comment" defends Reagan's Cancun message on aid self-sufficiency, praises the Bombay High Court's ruling against Antulay as proof of judicial independence, and calls Western sanctions on Poland symbolically warranted despite socialist-bloc hypocrisy on the issue.

Rama Swarup's "Red Disinformation" argues the US has fallen behind Soviet and Chinese propaganda efforts, describing a two-pronged Soviet campaign on NATO missile deployment and a Chinese campaign offering an illusory anti-Soviet partnership.

Rashmi Taneja's "Turkey in Turmoil" surveys Turkey seventeen months after the 1980 military coup, crediting Finance Minister Turgut Ozal's reforms with falling inflation while noting tens of thousands detained and dozens of death sentences.

Book reviews cover Minoo Masani's memoir Against the Tide, dwelling on his adversarial relationship with Nehru and the Swatantra Party's rise and decline, and Dhananjay Keer's biography of B. R. Ambedkar, recounting his campaigns against untouchability and 1956 conversion to Buddhism.
A reprinted piece from The Radical Humanist criticises the UGC's grant of "Deemed University" status to Satya Sai Baba's college at Puttaparthi as an abdication of secular, scientific standards.
A reprinted OPINION editorial condemns the Supreme Court's Judges Case ruling as a "gift" to Mrs. Gandhi establishing executive supremacy over the judiciary.

M. R. Masani's "Mea Culpa" apologises for the journal's recent irregularity, reveals the Democratic Research Service had decided to suspend Freedom First before reversing course, and announces resumption of monthly publication under new management.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "A Variety of Comment" questions the propriety of a Supreme Court judge informally discussing a pending judgment with journalist Arun Shourie, and asks how Indian prison conditions compare to improved amenities in Northern Ireland's Maze and Armagh prisons.
Rama Swarup examines India's deepening trade dependence on the Soviet Union, its largest trading partner by 1981, questioning whether Moscow's purchases reflect genuine demand or strategic aims.

S. S. Bankeshwar argues non-alignment is largely a myth since every ostensibly non-aligned country is effectively dependent on one superpower camp, citing India's selective silence on Soviet interventions.

Pran Nath Lekhi warns of KGB infiltration of Indian political life, citing a CPM leak allegedly traced to Soviet sources and claiming 14,000 Russian advisers are active in India without public scrutiny.
A satirical airport vignette reads Bombay's contradictory rules and unreliable information as symptomatic of a deeper Indian cultural indifference to logical consistency and follow-through.

A survey of German, French and British press opinion argues the Western European nuclear-freeze movement is substantially shaped by Soviet-aligned Communist organising rather than being purely spontaneous.

A. James McAdams marks the Berlin Wall's twentieth anniversary, tracing how East Germany transformed a structure privately conceded even by Khrushchev to be "ugly" into a source of state pride and economic stability.

Reprinted letters mark the 25th anniversary of the 1956 Hungarian uprising, drawing a line from Hungary through the Soviet invasions of Czechoslovakia and Afghanistan to pressure on Poland, while a review of D. R. Mankekar's book covers the New World Information Order debate.

Nissim Ezekiel's "The Voice of Separatism" condemns the Akali Dal's demand for a separate Punjab constitution modelled on Jammu and Kashmir, arguing greater state autonomy is legitimate but separatism dressed as autonomy is not.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "A Variety of Comment" covers the Law Commission's questionnaire floating a split of the Supreme Court seen as threatening judicial independence, and recounts J. K. Galbraith's public clashes with Milton Friedman and Arthur Laffer over monetarism.

S. S. Bankeshwar's "A National Alternative" credits the BJP alone among opposition parties with establishing independent credibility, tracing this to JP's success in bringing the RSS and Jan Sangh into India's national mainstream via the Janata experiment.

Rashmi Taneja's "The Falkland Islands Crisis" narrates the escalation from Argentina's flag-raising at South Georgia to Britain's naval deployment, situating General Galtieri's invasion within Argentina's domestic economic crisis.

Ram Swarup's "Soviet Media Sensitivity on Foreign Aid" documents a rare crack in Soviet press silence over the economic cost of meat shipments to Poland amid a third consecutive poor Soviet grain harvest.
Two "Voices" pieces cover criticism of politicised Marathi literary conferences and an argument that steep taxation and fare disparities are crushing India's politically aware middle-income group.

A review of L. J. Macfarlane's The Right to Strike is used to critique India's Maintenance of Essential Services Act, arguing the measure is unprovoked given falling strike losses and likely reflects government's inability to tackle inflation and corruption.

"The Sikkim Connection" reports on the political tension after the cremation of ex-Chogyal Palden Namgyal, when thousands proclaimed his son the 13th Chogyal, which New Delhi regarded as bordering on sedition.
Nissim Ezekiel's "The Peace-Mongers" attacks Western disarmament campaigners for a double standard that condemns NATO rearmament while giving unchallenged Soviet military build-up a pass.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "A Variety of Comment" covers a Heritage Foundation collection on intellectuals' hostility to free markets, the Hayflick cell-ownership dispute, and the harsh martial-law sentencing of Polish unionist Ewa Kubasiewicz.

M. R. Masani, responding to a reader's charge of double standards, concedes Freedom First's inconsistency on India's 1975 annexation of Sikkim while citing his and JP's efforts on Kashmir and Nagaland.

Rama Swarup's "The Falkland Islands Issue: How the Soviets Gain" argues Argentina's junta and the Soviet Politburo are using each other opportunistically, with Moscow gaining grain trade, arms sales and strategic advantage from the crisis.

Gordon Brook-Shepherd's reprinted "Why Salvador is not Reagan's Poland" rebuts Moscow's equivalence between Poland and El Salvador, arguing the West never armed guerrillas as the Soviet bloc armed Salvadoran ones.

Three book reviews cover Soviet propaganda on Afghanistan, a lawyers' committee report tracing Afghanistan's political history to the Soviet-installed Karmal government, and an edited volume of Indian journalists unanimously favouring expansion of freedom and decentralisation.

The ICFTU's May Day message demands the release of Solidarity members and withdrawal of Soviet SS-20 missiles, while a compiled digest covers North Korean labour camps, smuggled Solidarity testimony, and degrading conditions in Delhi's Tihar jail.

Nissim Ezekiel's "The Cultural Vacuum" argues India's institutional dysfunction stems from the absence of a shared democratic culture beneath the formal machinery of politics, calling for organic cultural revival rather than Westernisation.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "A Variety Of Comment" praises the BBC's defence of its Falklands coverage against government pressure, criticises continued opposition to Bombay's pavement-dweller clearances, and summarises an Amnesty report finding Uganda's human rights record unimproved under Milton Obote.

Alexander Solzhenitsyn's reprinted polemic attacks Western media's enforced cheerfulness and one-sided reporting for blinding it to communism's advance, arguing Western capitalism is unwittingly arming the "communist monster."

Rashmi Taneja's "The Middle-East In Flames" argues Iraq's real war aim against Iran was overthrowing Khomeini and pre-empting Shiite unrest, tracing the Gulf Arab states' alarmed formation of the Gulf Co-operation Council.
Rama Swarup criticises India's Kabul ambassador for defending Soviet "war aims" more zealously than the Soviets themselves, as Kabul Radio brands India an "enemy of the Afghan people."

Shanti Saroop Bansal reports defector Stanislav Levtjenko's claims that the KGB funds and directs Western European peace movements, detailing a Danish Communist Youth "Catalog" of disinformation tactics.

A review of an interdisciplinary poverty-studies volume appears alongside S. S. Bankeshwar's satirical "Open Letter" mocking rebel MLAs and professional defectors amid the 1982 Haryana and Himachal Pradesh floor-crossing crisis.

In an exclusive interview, Morarji Desai defends the Janata Party as the true "National Alternative" and Gandhian heir to Congress, argues democracy has failed in Pakistan and Bangladesh because Islam is a "dictatorial religion," and rejects a proposed India-Pakistan No-War Pact.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "A Variety of Comment" criticises Lord Denning's forced retirement as a capitulation to public bias and argues India's plan to abolish pharmaceutical brand names for generic prescribing will worsen, not solve, the spurious-drugs problem.

Nirmala Joshi's "Moscow-Islamabad-New Delhi" details Soviet objections to India-Pakistan normalisation, fearing it would downgrade the 1971 Indo-Soviet Treaty and free Pakistan to act against Baluchis, Pathans and Afghanistan.

Bhuchung K. Tsering's "Sino-Tibetan Relations" surveys secretive delegation diplomacy between the Tibetan government-in-exile and China, culminating in a 1982 Beijing visit and a Chinese offer to let Tibetans open a "Bureau" there.

Nissim Ezekiel's "The War in Lebanon" defends Israel's 1982 invasion as aimed at restoring Lebanese sovereignty rather than conquest, contrasting Israeli internal debate with the PLO's declared aim of destroying Israel.
A review of Shashi Tharoor's Reasons of State endorses its account of Indian foreign policy as incoherent and rooted in contradictory Nehru-era ideological premises.

S. A. A. Pinto's "The Root of All Evil" traces India's corruption and black money to the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act and licensing controls, calling for a new political party to tell the poor that socialism has failed.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "A Variety of Comment" praises Zaire's President Mobutu for defying Arab-African pressure over Israel ties, welcomes George Gilder's Wealth and Poverty as a defence of free enterprise, and reports mass executions under Iran's post-1979 regime exceeding official figures.

Arvind Deshpande's "The Autonomy Demand" poses open questions about how far India should devolve autonomy to states, warning greater autonomy could worsen parochialism and citing Kashmir, Punjab's Akalis and Kerala/West Bengal's Marxists as cautionary examples.
A tribute marks the Australian journal Quadrant's 25th anniversary, crediting Polish emigre Richard Krygier as its guiding figure since founding.
A reprinted Kenyan editorial by George Githii protests preventive detention and self-censorship in Kenya, explicitly likened by the accompanying commentary to India's own Emergency-era experience.
Rama Swarup's "The Elusive Sino-Soviet Detente" analyses Brezhnev's 1982 Tashkent overture to China and Beijing's dismissive response, concluding neither side genuinely seeks reconciliation.

A symposium report, "The Aged and Society," surveys the health, psychological and social dimensions of ageing in India, noting the erosion of elderly family members' traditional decision-making role despite the nominal persistence of joint families.

Nissim Ezekiel's "Welcome Farooq Abdullah!" sarcastically attacks the new Jammu & Kashmir Chief Minister's dismissal of his father's entire cabinet within 48 hours as symptomatic of a wider Indian pattern of purges dressed up as demonstrating leadership.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "A Variety of Comment" cites first-hand Lebanese testimony of PLO abuses in Sidon, criticises Indian journalists' selective outrage over the Bihar Press Bill given their own Emergency-era record, and notes the global human-rights movement's relative silence on persecuted Chinese intellectuals.

Rama Swarup's "Peking's Foreign Relations" analyses a leaked 1980 Chinese internal briefing paper describing Beijing's simultaneous "American card," latent "Soviet card" and "Europe-Japan card" diplomacy while demanding an end to US arms sales to Taiwan.
Geeta Doctor's "A Boy Named Satyam" recounts an encounter with a Sri Lankan flower-selling orphan boy near Nuwara Eliya, reflecting on the guilt provoked by tourism-driven child begging.
V. V. Deshpande's "A Wonder Tree" promotes mass cultivation of the fast-growing, nitrogen-fixing Leucaena tree for rural development, citing Maharashtra's adoption of it for social forestry.

P. M. Kamath reviews A. Appadorai's Domestic Roots of India's Foreign Policy, endorsing its thesis that India's non-alignment and Arab-friendly foreign policy are substantially explained by domestic factors like the size of its Muslim population.

Mary Thomas reviews the Second Press Commission's "Minute of Dissent," detailing the four dissenting members' opposition to delinking newspaper ownership and other majority recommendations, situating the debate against the Bihar Press Bill controversy.
